stateIncomeTaxWithholding.method: Method II exact calculation: net wages = wages - Table A (deduction + exemptions); then (net wages - column 3) x column 4 + column 5 from the period's table for the marital status. When annualized net wages reach the Method III threshold ($1,077,550 single, $2,155,350 married), use Method III: annualized net wages x the Method III rate / pay periods.

paidFamilyLeave.note: Employees contribute 0.432% of their wages each pay period until they reach $411.91 for the year with this employer. An employer may collect this from employees but doesn't have to (it can pay the cost itself); payroll deducts it. PFL wages are "the money rate at which employment... is recompensed under the contract of hiring" (commissions and bonuses included); how employee pre-tax deductions, tips and company contributions count is not stated, so paychecks with them are refused for PFL until sourced.

cite.ref: "For 2026, employees will contribute 0.432% of their gross wages per pay period, with a maximum annual contribution of $411.91." "The maximum employee contribution for each covered employer in 2026 is $411.91."
"The 2026 payroll contribution is 0.432% of an employee's wages each pay period and is capped at an annual maximum of $411.91."
Deduction and waiver: "An employer is allowed, but not required, to collect contributions from its employees to offset the cost of providing disability and Paid Family Leave benefits."

disabilityBenefits.note: Employees may be charged 0.5% of wages, up to $0.60 a week, toward the employer's disability benefits (DBL) policy; the employer may collect it but doesn't have to. Payroll doesn't deduct DBL yet (docs/open-questions.md): how the weekly cap applies to semimonthly and monthly pay, and which wages count, are not stated in the supplied sources. Employees receiving social security old-age benefits are exempt once they file Form DB-130.

cite.ref: Disability benefits: "An employee's contribution is computed at the rate of one-half of one percent of their wages, but no more than sixty cents a week." "An employer is allowed, but not required, to collect contributions from its employees"; employees entitled to old age insurance benefits "shall be exempt upon filing Form DB130 with the employer and the chair."
§ 201(12), definition of wages (as for Paid Family Leave)

workedExamples.discrepancy: The tables give $258.50: $165.00 x 0.0753 = $12.4245, which rounds to $12.42, but the booklet shows $12.43. The other six examples round to the nearest cent, so this is a one-cent error in the booklet; the engine follows the tables.

The tables give $248.12: $58.80 x 0.0707 = $4.157, which rounds to $4.16, but the booklet prints the rate as 0.070 and the result as $4.15. A one-cent error in the booklet; the engine follows the tables.

$3,576.63 x 0.1675 = $599.0855, which rounds to $599.09; the booklet shows $599.08, although on the same page $44.10 x 0.1675 = $7.38675 is rounded up to $7.39. A one-cent inconsistency in the booklet; the engine rounds to the nearest cent.

incomeTax.note: New York State, New York City and Yonkers withholding apply to the wages subject to federal income tax withholding.

cite.ref: E. Income subject to withholding: "Compensation that is considered as wages for federal income tax withholding purposes, including tips... is generally considered wages for purposes of withholding New York State income tax, New York City income tax, Yonkers resident tax surcharge, and Yonkers nonresident earnings tax"

"Contributions to a qualified cash or deferred salary profit-sharing or stock bonus plan which are excluded from an employee's income for federal income tax purposes are also excluded from income for New York State and City of New York income tax purposes. Accordingly, such contributions are not subject to New York State or City of New York income tax withholding."

publicEmployees.note: Public employees' 414(h) retirement contributions and New York City's own flexible benefits program (IRC 125) are added back on the employee's New York return. Payroll has no item kinds for these public-employer plans, so they are not supported.

cite.ref: 414(h) contributions and NYC flexible benefits program amounts are reported as addition modifications on Form IT-201/IT-203

unemployment.note: Salaries, commissions, bonuses, certified tips and the reasonable value of noncash pay (taxable fringe benefits) are remuneration. Employer payments under a plan for retirement or for medical or hospitalization expenses, and payments to a 401(a) trust, are not. Employee pre-tax deductions (401(k), cafeteria plan, FSA, HSA) are not addressed by § 517 or the Department of Labor sources supplied, so paychecks with them are refused for New York unemployment until sourced. Dismissal (severance) payments are excluded by § 517(2)(h); payroll has no severance kind, so don't pay severance with an earnings kind until one is added.

cite.ref: Remuneration "includes every form of compensation paid to covered employees including salary, cash wages, commissions, bonuses, tips, vacation pay..."

Payments to employees not reportable: "Any payment made under a plan or system providing for retirement, sickness, or accident disability, or medical or hospital expenses for an employee... including amounts paid for insurance"; "Payments from or to a trust described in IRC § 401(a)"

§ 517(1): "'Remuneration' means every form of compensation for employment paid by an employer to his employee... including salaries, commissions, bonuses, and the reasonable money value of board, rent, housing, lodging, or similar advantage received." § 517(2) exclusions include (a) plan payments "on account of retirement, or sickness or accident disability, or medical or hospitalization expenses", (e) payments "from or to a trust described in section four hundred one (a)" and (h) "Dismissal payments."

Reporting Tips: "The amount certified by employees must be included in the employer's quarterly contribution reports"; page 2: "The reasonable value of any noncash compensation provided by employers to their employees is remuneration which is reportable and subject to contribution on a quarterly basis."

paidFamilyLeave.note: Pay for services; other kinds are not addressed by the supplied PFL sources.

cite.ref: "0.432% of their gross wages per pay period"

§ 201(12): "'Wages' means the money rate at which employment with a covered employer is recompensed under the contract of hiring with the covered employer and shall include the reasonable value of board, rent, housing, lodging, or similar advantage received under the contract of hiring." Supplied with it, from paidfamilyleave.ny.gov/cost: "Commissions and bonuses are considered wages for PFL purposes."
